item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs

item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.title: Federal judge rules against administration in American Samoa seabed mining lease

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: NWS urges vigilance as dry season begins across Guam and CNMI

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade
item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal.

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade winds, according to the National Weather Service in Guam. Fire danger on Guam has risen to the high category as rainfall remains limited and vegetation continues to dry out.

Despite the dry conditions, Marcus Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Guam office, said residents should not overlook the threat of tropical cyclones.

"The risk for late-season tropical cyclones remains elevated through the end of the year and into early 2027 compared with other years," Aydlett said, citing the ongoing El Niño pattern.

No tropical cyclone development is expected during the next seven days, but forecasters said El Niño conditions could continue to influence weather across the western Pacific through the remainder of the year.

The weather service said a wetter pattern may develop later next week and continue into December, providing some relief to drought-affected areas across Micronesia. Residents with low or empty water catchments are encouraged to collect rainwater when showers occur.

item.content:encoded:
Sylvester Stallone's underdog story Rocky was crowned the Best Picture at the 1977 Academy Awards. The film's most famous sequence shows the character Rocky Balboa training for his big heavyweight boxing championship.

He runs through trainyards, a crowded outdoor market, and a jogging path. He punches a speedbag, does push-ups and sit-ups, gets repeatedly jabbed in the stomach, and slugs frozen sides of beef with his bare knuckles. Finally, Rocky sprints up the steps of the Philadelphia Art Museum, all the way to the top, where he jumps up and down and raises his arms in triumph.

Now the new movie I Play Rocky tells the story about how Stallone wrote and starred in his movie. It also celebrates the original cinematographer, Garrett Brown . He invented the Steadicam — which is still in use today.

For Rocky , Brown used his invention to shoot from inside the boxing ring; he also wove through the frozen meat locker and ran up those steps with Rocky.

"He's not just holding a camera, he's telling a story," says I Play Rocky director Peter Farrelly. Garrett's smooth camera movements captured Rocky's iconic moment at the top of the stairs that still — a half-century later — has fans cheering wildly.

"Garrett Brown was smart enough and savvy enough and artistic enough," says Farrelly, "[that] he didn't just shoot him going up the stairs, he followed him around and we got to be part of it as an audience."

All the while, Brown was filming with his invention strapped to his chest.

"It has a harness instead of being in your hands," Brown tells NPR about his Steadicam. "And at the business end of that arm is a so-called gimbal, so that any angular thing that I did not get through to the camera."

Brown's contraption included a fiber optic viewfinder strapped to his head. "I can only imagine what that looked like," he chuckles. "You have to be immune to embarrassment to try out inventions like that."

Brown's Steadicam earned him an Oscar in 1978. He went on to invent the Skycam , a flying camera for capturing live sports. He also invented the Mobycam and the Divecam for filming sports underwater, along with other camera innovations that have revolutionized cinematography.

But Brown actually started out in music, imitating the Kingston Trio in high school. In college, he met Alfred Dana Arioli, and they became the folk-singing duo Brown and Dana . They even sang and recorded the song " It Was a Very Good Year " two years before Frank Sinatra's version won a Grammy.

"We were pretty good. We recorded for MGM and did college concerts all around and so on," Brown reminisces. "For me, that ended with a car crash on the way from a gig in Winnipeg. Then the Beatles came out. We looked at each other and thought: 'we are toast.'"

Brown got out of folk music, and for a time was selling cars while teaching himself to become a filmmaker.

He started his own production company and began creating live-action videos for Sesame Street in the 1960s.

Brown also came up with new ways to shoot commercials.

"I did invent a weird, wonderful dog's eye view dolly," he says. "My little device made a very realistic point of view of a beagle. That intrigued the hell out of me."

Brown says he was fed up with the bigger, cumbersome dollies used to pull cameras. And he found handheld cameras too jerky.

"If you taped a camera to your head, which the French New Wave guys did, it looks horrible, very unlike what humans see," he says, "You know, we don't see it bouncing like that. We see it smooth."

Brown says he locked himself in a hotel room for a week in 1974 until he came up with a sketch for the Steadicam.

Then with his invention, he went all around Philadelphia taking what he called " 30 impossible shots. "

Those test shots caught the attention of filmmakers.

In 1976, Brown and his Steadicam wandered through a labor camp following the Woody Guthrie characters for the movie Bound for Glory .

Brown's "30 impossible shots" included him following his then-girlfriend — now wife Ellen, as she ran up those steps of the Philadelphia Art Museum. The same steps used in Rocky . You can see that original footage in the new film about Rocky.

For the 1983 Star Wars film Return of the Jedi , Brown walked through a redwood forest shooting slower than one frame a second with his Steadicam. Speeded up, it created the 100 mph chase scene.

Later, Stanley Kubrick used Brown and his Steadicam for his 1980 horror film The Shining . The inventor has since shot many other films, including Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom .

Brown says the Steadicam replicates the native human look, which is stable.

"It turns out that our eyes are internally stabilized by our inner ear," he says. "In fact, your human eye looks very much like a Steadicam, because when you walk, you don't even see yourself go up and down. You see a very smooth shot."

Brown says his invention takes a very skilled human to operate — something that could never be done realistically by AI.

item.title: Armand Hammer has what it takes to outlast the end times

item.content:encoded:
Techno-feudalist hellscape got you feeling hopeless? There's likely an Armand Hammer lyric for that.

Throughout a slow-building 13-year career, the witty, polemical New York rap duo has built a catalog out of prescient observations that call you to join in raging against the machine. If you're thinking of taking up arms against classism or the carceral state, Elucid would like a word: "The lower the wage, the bigger the gauge is / With no regard to rising inflation / Doublin' down on shackling multiple generations in cages," he rapped on 2017's " Barbarians ." If you're grappling with the West's complicity in a destabilized political landscape, billy woods is fully disgusted on behalf of the Global South: "The world doesn't turn anymore / Half burns, the other side will never thaw, burning books to keep warm," goes last year's " Laraaji ." From biometrics ("I feel a way about provin' my identity to robots") to machine learning ("Tears in my eyes listening to machines make music"), few artists are more uniquely tapped into just how automated our autocracy has become, or how absurd it all can feel.

There's a new all-timer line to add to that list: "Surveillance state bite hard like old man winter / Chipped teeth, white meat, bone slivers / Unfortunately it's not 'if,' but 'when' they gon' kill us," Elucid raps on " Nightswim ," an ominous cut from the new Armand Hammer album, Snakes & Ladders . His voice inches out of a fog, from conspiratorial to snarling, facing down what woods later describes as "capitalism's gaping maw." But that's not where the story ends: "When the blood of the righteous run like rain in the street / Wave ripple in the wind, between your toes, beneath my feet," he continues, the song surging toward an interpolation of C-Murder's "Down 4 My N's." The mood is not defeatism but pragmatism, a well-earned suspicion about achieving the solidarity that a fight for equity requires. "Nightswim" betrays a truth about its creators: While their music is penned like literature, it is defined in the space beyond words. Everything they make is intentionally on-edge and off-kilter, but this album is a monument to the singular way their songs exploit pockets of sound and meaning to render a dimension all their own, one that continues to rally adherents to its cause.

If it's true that, as William S. Burroughs once put it, "a paranoid might be defined as someone who has some idea as to what is actually going on," the music on Snakes & Ladders is deeply paranoid, and its architects clearly know a great deal — about what is actually going on, and also how to weaponize art in class struggle. Solidarity takes many forms; here, it is an organizing effort, bringing producers from across both rappers' discographies into a craggy coalition. In this sense, Snakes & Ladders presents a gripping argument for Armand Hammer as the defining rap group of its era — not simply because its music is perfectly equipped to grapple with our eye-in-the-sky political reality, but because the sound itself is dystopian, if also clear-eyed and dryly funny. In gathering many of the pair's essential beatmakers, the album showcases the ways their tenacity has borne fruit: a hard-won and truly indie style, an unmistakable chemistry, a cooperative community and a real cult following. The songs both bear witness and demand attention be paid: "The meek inherit the Earth, when? 'Cause this I gots to see," woods cries out incredulously on " Incidentals ." This is punchy noise rap imagined as a self-sustaining, Afro-pessimistic free-jazz co-op.

Even beyond its two albums with loop legend The Alchemist , Armand Hammer has amassed a cohort of collaborators accomplished in their niches, all of whom have helped outline the group's pre-cataclysmic sound. With Al busy cooking up for the witch doctor Erykah Badu, the rest of the roster — including standouts Kenny Segal, Preservation, Animoss and Child Actor — contributes to an astonishing collage of askew tunes and freaked-out rhythms. The last Armand Hammer album, last year's solo Alchemist-produced Mercy , was a bit more straight-on with its palette, which could be cold while still dialed-in and groovy. Snakes & Ladders has a more anarchic feel. It isn't free jazz in any literal sense, though songs like the flittering " Jet Magazine " and the ecstatic " Times Tables " channel the chaos in various ways — but it is in a functional one. The music defies rap formalism; sonically, it prioritizes the unconventional and atonal, and few rappers are able to swing cadences quite like these experimental technicians.

The great hip-hop duos — Mobb Deep, OutKast, Black Star, UGK, Clipse — are all defined by the polarity of their internal dynamic, the particular friction of their juxtaposed styles that drums up an inherent drama. Elucid and woods are challenging characters who don't shy away from axe-grinding Socratic dialogue, and the friction in their work could start a data-center fire. Elucid is the crusader, woods the stoicist, yet they each have some of the other's quality in them. The former is militant and emphatic, bluesy and syncopated like a slam poet, the latter covert and elegiac, freewheeling and diagnostic like a color commentator for the blood sport of American politics. They are simultaneously at variance with one another and always on the same wavelength.

To anyone paying attention, woods has been climbing the list of best-ever rappers for some time , but Snakes & Ladders proves for good that Elucid is far more than just his ideal running mate. Armand Hammer's grouchier half is an utter force of nature here, with verses that press into you and leave a mark. As he barrels through the cavernous production on " Lock Out/Tag Out ," its keys dripping like water off stalactites, each enunciated syllable crackles like a firecracker in the dark. Later, on the buzzing, machine-powered " Assembly Lines ," he becomes a soothsayer, taking purported futurists as omens to see past A.I. propaganda: "Ray Kurzweil's wet dreams spray like puppy water on corporate salad slop / Your favorite flavor optimization / The cage is electric, the cruelty baseless / The sacred smooth down like dripping water shaping stone, faceless," he chants, the flow so free-associative that the phrases begin to feel like a Rorschach test.

It would be easy to write Armand Hammer off as prophets of doom. "Put aside your calculations, baby, this the time of oracles / Power of suggestion, weapon in your face, questions is rhetorical / Count my blessings, nevertheless, yes, everything's horrible," woods raps on " Dragon Teeth ," not exactly putting lipstick on the pig. Wade deeper into the murky waters, though, and you'll discover an undaunted spirit: The game is the game and you can't play scared, as woods tells us . You can hear that ideal on " Dogville ," in which woods imagines an alternate future — equity and justice instead of bombs, emptied prisons, no hunger, peace, renewal — before crashing back into the reality of the outside world: dilapidated trains, "lepers" pleading, police like wild dogs, kids getting mobbed outside the corner store. He's had enough. "No more talk," he snaps. "You can't talk over that belt feed / I don't sleep, I don't dream / Mouse frantic in the maze / But the snake moves with ease." The duo has held up its end, saying all there is to say. There are only so many Armand Hammer lyrics you can absorb before you get the message.

item.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
item.description: A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground. item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement .

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.

That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered .

Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location , saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.

The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

In court filings and a recently unveiled website , the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security . Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week , Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda , including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.

Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday . That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.

Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.

The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.

Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

item.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
item.description: Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts. Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
item.content:encoded:
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?

When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me , and she still has her ."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.

Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.

I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn . She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection , where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.

Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?

The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six .

Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.

Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.

Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.

Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.

Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.

Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.

State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.

Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.

"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.

Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."

It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.

Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.

Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?

Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order . Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.

As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."

So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

For more, follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
